name: Spinning Round (Easy Version)
description: This is the easy version of the problem. The only difference between the two versions are the allowed characters in $$$s$$$. In the easy version, $$$s$$$ only contains the character ? . You can make hacks only if both versions of the problem are solved. You are given a permutation $$$p$$$ of length $$$n$$$. You are also given a string $$$s$$$ of length $$$n$$$, consisting only of the character ? . For each $$$i$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$: Define $$$l_i$$$ as the largest index $$$j \lt i$$$ such that $$$p_j \gt p_i$$$. If there is no such index, $$$l_i := i$$$. Define $$$r_i$$$ as the smallest index $$$j \gt i$$$ such that $$$p_j \gt p_i$$$. If there is no such index, $$$r_i := i$$$. Initially, you have an undirected graph with $$$n$$$ vertices (numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$) and no edges. Then, for each $$$i$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$, add one edge to the graph: If $$$s_i =$$$ L , add the edge $$$(i, l_i)$$$ to the graph. If $$$s_i =$$$ R , add the edge $$$(i, r_i)$$$ to the graph. If $$$s_i =$$$ ? , either add the edge $$$(i, l_i)$$$ or the edge $$$(i, r_i)$$$ to the graph at your choice. Find the maximum possible diameter$$$^{\text{∗}}$$$ over all connected graphs that you can form. Output $$$-1$$$ if it is not possible to form any connected graphs. $$$^{\text{∗}}$$$ Let $$$d(s, t)$$$ denote the smallest number of edges on any path between $$$s$$$ and $$$t$$$. The diameter of the graph is defined as the maximum value of $$$d(s, t)$$$ over all pairs of vertices $$$s$$$ and $$$t$$$.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line of input contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 2 \cdot 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 4 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the length of the permutation $$$p$$$. The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$p_1,p_2,\ldots, p_n$$$ ($$$1 \le p_i \le n$$$) — the elements of $$$p$$$, which are guaranteed to form a permutation. The third line of each test case contains a string $$$s$$$ of length $$$n$$$. It is guaranteed that it consists only of the character ? . It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$4 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output the maximum possible diameter over all connected graphs that you form, or $$$-1$$$ if it is not possible to form any connected graphs.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1987G1 — Spinning Round (Easy Version) [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
